data.q_1: Thermal Runaway in lithium ion batteries is a uncontrollable, self heating state of the battery where the internal temperature increases much more and faster than the battery can cool. A thermal runaway can primarily be triggered by physically puncturing or breaking a battery. When the battery s triggered, the battery's electrodes short circuit and generate intense localized heat. This heat causes the battery's protective components and highly volatile electrolyte to break down, releasing their own stored oxygen. This combination of both the extreme heat and the sudden released oxygen, rapidly accelerates the chemical breakdown of the battery. Though this is what a thermal runaway is, how the damaged battery ignites is not far from this as the runaway cycle rapidly increases the chemical breakdown of the battery, it also vaporizes the battery's flammable liquid electrolyte. Thus, when the realized oxygen, intense heat, and flammable vapor come together a jet of flame or a explosive release of gases is created by bursting the case. When these lithium-ion batteries are improperly disposed along with our normal trash, they cause intense fires and hard to extinguish fires in landfills as the batteries are punctured, crushed, or short circuited by heavy missionary activating the thermal runaway of the lithium-ion battery.
data.q_2: The Democratic Republic of Congo produces approximately 75% of the world's total mined cobalt. The working conditions are full of risk and danger especially in the artisanal and small scale mining sectors where thousands of people including thousands of children, mine for minerals in unregulated, toxic and dangerous environments. The human rights concerns in the mining sectors of the DRC are child and forced labor, unsafe and deadly working conditions, toxic exposure and health risks. Approximately 40 thousand children, as young as seven, work in the DRC's artisanal cobalt mines, with many dropping out of school to mine minerals in 12 hour shifts for as little as a dollar per day. Miners mostly work by hand in the deep tunnels without basic protective equipment with mine collapses and fatal accidents being a frequent occurrence. This is tied to recycling as recycling the dead batteries from electronics, electric vehicle directly recovers the cobalt present in them. This cobalt retrieved from already used batteries can significantly reduce the global reliance on newly mined materials. By replacing the newly mined cobalt with the cobalt retrieved from the old batteries, that were recycled. This can heavily mitigate the severe environmental degradation and human rights exploitation from new mining operations.
data.q_3: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is a environmental policy that puts the financial and physical responsibility of product disposal specifically end of life products from the municipalities and taxpayers to the producers of the products. This policy is also active in Nova Scotia for batteries, meaning the producers of the batteries are legally responsible for financing and managing the recycling and the collection of their batteries (in this case batteries). This EPR is legally stated under the Nova Scotia Solid Waste-Resource Management Regulations with the government approved battery stewardship program in Nova Scotia being managed by Call2Recycle Canada.
